title: Initialization-generation fair-slice controller: adaptive phase splitting to balance latency, throughput, and tenant fairness
creator: Avery Chen
description:
Background: Our serving runtime currently treats model request work as two conceptual stages: initialization (tokenization/prefill-like steps that build an initial KV cache and compute key attention state) and generation (autoregressive decode). Existing schedulers either statically split these phases or aggressively fuse them which causes worst-case tail latency for latency-sensitive tenants and suboptimal throughput utilization for batch-oriented tenants.

Goal: Design and implement an adaptive 'fair-slice controller' that: 1) dynamically decides phase splitting (split vs fused) per-request using a lightweight cost model and kernel/attention hints; 2) surfaces kernel-selection signals (e.g., transposed GEMM vs fused attention kernels) to the slice allocator; 3) enforces soft fairness policies across tenants to reduce tail latency regressions without sacrificing too much throughput.

Success metrics (initial):
- Median end-to-end latency for latency-tier requests improves by >= 10% under mixed workloads.
- P99 latency regression for top 10% tenants <= 5% vs baseline.
- Overall token throughput drop <= 8% in the worst-case fairness enforcement scenario.
- Jain's fairness index across tenant latencies improves by 0.05 (measured per-window).

Design summary:
- Lightweight cost estimator: use per-model profile (sequence-length histogram, attention memory growth, kernel latency table) + a micro-probe at request arrival to estimate whether fusing phases or splitting will yield better tenant-level utility under current queue lengths.
- Soft-slice policy: if estimated completion time for fused path exceeds tenant SLO headroom, controller will split phase into a short initialization slice (fast kernels, high priority) and a lower-priority generation slice. Otherwise, it will favor fused execution to improve throughput.
- Kernel hints: scheduler will annotate slices with kernel preferences (e.g., prefer quantized matmul path, use sparse-attention kernel, or request packed KV cache path). Kernel selection table will be consulted by the runtime to pick the fastest-compatible kernel.
- Attention optimism: for initialization slices we will probe whether we can use reduced-context attention windows (trim leading context) or shared prefix caching to reduce memory movement and enable smaller kernel footprints.
- Fairness enforcement: implement a tenant-credit soft-gating mechanism (per-tenant latency credits). Credits are debited when a tenant accumulates tail latency and are earned back slowly. Controller uses credits to choose whether to prioritize their initialization slices.

Trading points and rationale:
- Why not always split? Splitting adds scheduling overhead and may increase total compute (more kernel launches), hurting throughput. The adaptive estimator prevents unnecessary splits.
- Why not always fuse? Fusion is efficient for throughput but leads to head-of-line blocking by long initialization steps; soft fairness reduces this.
- Kernel hinting increases complexity at the scheduler/runtime contract boundary but yields 10-20% kernel-level wins in internal microbenchmarks.

Implementation plan:
1) Add model profile metadata: sequence-length distribution, representative kernel latency table (on each hardware class). (Spike done)
2) Implement micro-probe: a lightweight probe that runs a tiny attention cost estimate on arrival (PR: github.com/redwood/runtime/pull/1796). (PR open)
3) Controller logic in scheduler: cost estimator + decision function + credit account. Unit tests and simulator harness.
4) Runtime kernel hint plumbing: accept slice hints and consult kernel-selection table at launch.
5) Canary rollout: 5% cluster traffic with telemetry collection (p50/p90/p99, throughput, credit balance drift).

Acceptance criteria: 
- End-to-end integration test in staging that reproduces a 60/40 mix of latency/throughput tenants and shows improved fairness index.
- No P99 regression longer than 5% for any tenant in the canary cluster after 48h.
- Observability: per-slice metrics emitted (decision=split|fused, chosen_kernel, estimated_cost, actual_duration).

Risks and mitigations: 
- Mis-estimation: micro-probe could mis-predict for out-of-distribution prompts. Mitigate with fallback: controller will back off to conservative default (fuse) and record telemetry.
- Kernel availability mismatches: some hardware may not have preferred kernels; runtime will gracefully fall back. Add unit tests that assert fallback path correctness.
- Billing/chargeback complexity: splitting may change token accounting. Work with billing to ensure token attribution remains consistent.

Related artifacts: design doc, simulator outputs, microbench tables.
